title: The Winners, Losers From USMNT’s Faultless World Cup Return
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom12:30 PM EDTCavan Sullivan (left) and Christian Pulisic have had a very different few weeks. / Omar Vega/USSF/Getty Images (Sullivan), Marco Luzzani/Getty Images (Pulisic)Mauricio Pochettino may have extended his stay at the U.S. men’s national team but the Argentine manager has made it abundantly clear that this is very much a new regime. The program would be “starting from zero” he warned.

Four wins while jumping around five states in three time zones has afforded Pochettino’s new project the perfect platform from which to build. Results were never at the forefront of the manager’s mind but a faultless return from a somewhat underwhelming World Cup on home soil has given some time for experimentation.

Almost every gamble which Pochettino made paid off during a series of wildly varied victories over Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada. Yet, for each winner on the roster, there was a bitter victim of the USMNT’s success watching from the sidelines.

From Russell Crowe to Mick Jagger, Mauricio Pochettino has changed his fashion choices this fall. / David Berding/USSF/Getty ImagesAfter signing a bumper contract through the 2030 World Cup, Pochettino is in a position of power. Nevertheless, a less daring manager would perhaps have picked at least one of Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie or Folarin Balogun and fewer than 13 uncapped youngsters. However, Pochettino is in the business of blooding a new generation of talent. There is no time to lose and he came through the biggest leap of faith without a single “L” to his name.
Beyond the tally of 12 goals scored and three conceded across the four straight wins, the USMNT retained that full-throttle approach which has defined the nation’s best performances under Pochettino.

“We played four games in two weeks, and to play always with the same intensity, with the same commitment, with the same passion, that is a thing that we keep,” the demanding manager understandably beamed.
To be the future you must rewrite history. pic.twitter.com/MID0hojIEy

Cavan Sullivan was not the USMNT’s best performer this fall; he wasn’t even the best teenager on the roster. However, it is Philadelphia Union’s peroxide-blonde 17-year-old who has been the face of this window for his dexterity as well as his industry.

Pochettino’s star pupil played with an infectious energy which coursed through the entire team. His record-breaking goal against Mexico may have come from a boneheaded blunder by goalkeeper Raúl Rangel, yet the modern perception of players is so often a collection of moments rather than a monument to consistency. Sullivan delivered the clippable content while also running hard enough to win the approval of Pochettino. Job done.
The USMNT are handing the keys to the kids. pic.twitter.com/cpWbBzfEFb
There were 13 players on Pochettino’s roster who started the international window without a single senior cap. By the end of the intense schedule, the entire baker’s dozen had been given a run-out.
“I think obviously there are a lot of new faces, and they all had great energy and worked very hard while they were here,” mused Gio Reyna, a veritable veteran at the ripe old age of 23.

The hard work doesn’t stop here. If this kindergarten class hopes to have any chance of being reunited in November, their toughest job is only just getting started. “The most difficult thing is how we support these young players,” Pochettino explained.

“The easier thing always is to arrive there and make their debut. But now, how we are going to evolve with them, and how we are going to protect [them]? ... How are we going to make them understand that now they have more responsibility? That is one of the things that we were talking [about] in the dressing room, too.”

Gio Reyna has always been a Mauricio Pochettino favorite. / Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesAvailability is the best quality and one which has been lacking for so much of Reyna’s young but tumultuous career. However, this window offered some unprecedented whiffs of consistency. Pochettino’s pet project was an ever-present member of an ever-changing starting XI.

That quartet of starts followed on from a run of form for Strasbourg which has now seen Reyna start eight straight matches for club and country for the first time in his entire senior career. For context, he made his professional debut in January 2020.

Rather than dwell on that landmark, Reyna shifted the focus forward. “Honestly, [I’m] more just thinking about keep going now ... just keep building what I’ve been doing, keep showing up every day, training, recovering, doing everything I need to prepare mentally and physically for every training and game,” he shrugged.
“[I] feel good, though. Feeling more confident every time I step on the pitch. It was a good amount of minutes, so just very happy with obviously how this window went, as well.”

Christian Pulisic was not called up. / Giuseppe Maffia/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesIt’s easy to cast those who fall in the shadows of angels as devils. A fully fit and scoring Christian Pulisic was left at home and the biggest story was that it wasn’t much of a story at all.
